## Exploratory DSEM Recruitment Pathways

This section is the indicator-analysis pilot within a draft EBS pollock
Ecosystem and Socioeconomic Profile (ESP), rather than an attempt to estimate
the full pollock early-survival system. The BSAI Groundfish Plan Team
recommended in 2021 that an EBS walleye pollock ESP be added to the list of
future ESPs [@npfmc2021bsai]. The analysis follows the
sequence recommended in the AFSC causal-modeling guidance: define the outcome,
build a literature-based mechanism table and generic DAG, select a small set of
scientifically defensible graphs, retain a no-edge baseline, and compare all
graphs on the same data [@monnahan2026causalpractices]. The mechanism table and
DAG draw on the January 2025 pollock workshop, the age-0 pollock working-group
material, and the Tiger Team data-availability synthesis
[@monnahan2026pollockworkshop; @siddon2026age0pollock; @afsc2026age0dag;
@ianelli2026tigerteam] and the
[EBS pollock Early Survival Pathways synthesis](https://afsc-assessments.github.io/ebswp_esp/)
[@ianelli2026ebswpesp].

The response is the Rceattle age-1 recruitment state. The two examples test
late-summer SST in the cohort's age-0 year and cold-pool extent in the following
age-1 calendar year. They were selected because both have relatively long
annual records and represent distinct, prespecified hypotheses. The analysis
does not treat them as direct measurements of prey quality, energetic
condition, cannibalism, or survival.

### ESP development scope

The September product documents the justification, synthesis, generic DAG,
mechanism table, and two illustrative fits. It does not substitute a long list
of available covariates for a small set of causal hypotheses. The intended
progression identifies the completed September analyses and the work deferred
to November (@tbl-esp-development-scope). The full draft ESP structure is
provided in Appendix A-3.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-esp-development-scope
#| tbl-cap: "Development scope for the EBS pollock ESP and its Rceattle-DSEM indicator analysis."
#| tbl-pos: "H"

tibble::tribble(
  ~Component, ~September_draft, ~November_target,
  "Justification and outcome", "Document the Plan Team request and define age-1 recruitment as the focal population response.", "Confirm the focal response and management use with the ESP team.",
  "Indicator synthesis", "Provide a life-history synthesis, generic DAG, mechanism table, and data-availability review.", "Update indicators through the ESP and Ecosystem Status Report data-collection process.",
  "Candidate hypotheses", "Retain two transparent proxy examples: age-0 late-summer SST and cold-pool extent.", "Fit two to five defensible candidate DAGs that represent proximal mediators where data permit.",
  "Indicator analysis", "Compare the two single-edge examples and their combined diagnostic with the no-edge IID reference.", "Add predictive, retrospective, timing, and observation-error checks to the candidate-DAG comparison.",
  "Management use", "Use results to illustrate the integrated Rceattle-DSEM workflow and identify data gaps.", "Determine whether validated indicators are suitable for operational recruitment modeling or risk-table context."
) |>
  gt() |>
  cols_label(
    September_draft = "September draft",
    November_target = "November target"
  ) |>
  cols_width(
    Component ~ px(135),
    September_draft ~ px(275),
    November_target ~ px(275)
  ) |>
  tab_options(table.font.size = px(9))
```

### Mechanism table and generic DAG

The reduced mechanism table distinguishes processes that can be tested with the
current annual data from biologically important mediators that remain
intermittent or unavailable (@tbl-dsem-mechanisms). Expected signs describe the
direction from the listed driver toward age-1 recruitment, whether directly or
through the stated mechanism.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-dsem-mechanisms
#| tbl-cap: "Reduced mechanism table for the illustrative age-0 to age-1 recruitment analysis. Coverage refers to the cohort-aligned data presently available to this working paper."
#| tbl-pos: "H"

tibble::tribble(
  ~Driver, ~Mechanism, ~Expected_sign, ~Current_coverage, ~Role_in_this_section,
  "Sea ice", "Winter ice affects summer cold-pool extent, bloom conditions, and prey production.", "Indirect", "Annual physical index available; not fitted here", "Upstream context",
  "Cold-pool extent", "A larger cold pool can separate juveniles from adult pollock and reduce cannibalism.", "Positive", sprintf("%d annual values", sum(is.finite(dsem_covariates$ColdPool))), "Illustrative proxy edge",
  "Age-0 late-summer SST", "Warmer water can increase metabolic demand and reduce energy stored before winter.", "Negative", sprintf("%d annual values", sum(is.finite(dsem_covariates$LateSummerSST))), "Illustrative proxy edge",
  "Large copepods and euphausiids", "Lipid-rich prey supports age-0 growth, energy storage, and overwinter survival.", "Positive", "Intermittent; 15 values in the current ESP cohort table", "Unfitted mediator",
  "Fall age-0 energy", "Higher energy density and total energy increase overwinter survival to age 1.", "Positive", "Absent from the current annual cohort table", "Priority mediator",
  "Adult-pollock overlap", "Greater adult-juvenile overlap increases cannibalism exposure.", "Negative", "A separate range-overlap product exists, but its survey timing is contemporaneous with the age-1 state", "Deferred from the main example"
) |>
  gt() |>
  cols_width(
    Driver ~ px(90),
    Mechanism ~ px(205),
    Expected_sign ~ px(65),
    Current_coverage ~ px(145),
    Role_in_this_section ~ px(95)
  ) |>
  cols_label(
    Expected_sign = "Expected sign",
    Current_coverage = "Current coverage",
    Role_in_this_section = "Role here"
  ) |>
  tab_options(table.font.size = px(8))
```

The generic DAG is adapted from the age-0 pollock working-group graph and
retains both bottom-up and top-down routes (@fig-dsem-dag). It makes the
unobserved or intermittent mediators visible instead of allowing the two
available physical proxies to stand in for entire mechanisms. Solid arrows are
conceptual. Dashed arrows are the only recruitment paths fitted in this proof
of concept.

```{mermaid}
%%| label: fig-dsem-dag
%%| fig-cap: "Generic directed acyclic graph for eastern Bering Sea pollock survival from age 0 to age 1. Solid arrows summarize hypothesized mechanisms. Dashed arrows are the two direct proxy paths fitted in the illustrative Rceattle-DSEM comparison."
%%| fig-alt: "Sea ice influences cold-pool extent, summer temperature, bloom conditions, and prey. Prey and juvenile abundance influence age-0 energy, which affects overwinter survival. Cold-pool extent, juvenile distribution, and adult pollock affect cannibalism exposure. Overwinter survival and predation survival lead to age-1 recruitment. Dashed arrows connect late-summer SST and cold-pool extent directly to recruitment for the two illustrative fitted hypotheses."
%%| fig-width: 6.3
%%| fig-pos: H
flowchart LR
  ICE["Winter<br/>sea ice"] --> COLD["Summer<br/>cold pool"]
  ICE --> BLOOM["Bloom timing<br/>and production"]
  ICE --> SST["Age-0 late-<br/>summer SST"]

  BLOOM --> PREY["Large copepods<br/>and euphausiids"]
  SST --> PREY
  PREY --> A0["Age-0 abundance,<br/>growth, and size"]
  PREY --> ENERGY["Age-0 diet lipid,<br/>energy density,<br/>and total energy"]
  A0 --> ENERGY
  ENERGY --> WINTER["Overwinter<br/>survival"]

  COLD --> SEP["Juvenile-adult<br/>spatial separation"]
  A0 --> JLOC["Juvenile<br/>distribution"]
  JLOC --> OVER["Cannibalism<br/>exposure"]
  SEP --> OVER
  ADULT["Adult pollock<br/>biomass and distribution"] --> OVER
  OVER --> PSURV["Predation<br/>survival"]

  WINTER --> REC["Age-1<br/>recruitment"]
  PSURV --> REC

  SST -. "fitted proxy edge" .-> REC
  COLD -. "fitted proxy edge" .-> REC

  classDef physical fill:#e8f2f7,stroke:#26739b,stroke-width:2px,color:#1f2933;
  classDef prey fill:#ecf5eb,stroke:#6b8f24,stroke-width:2px,color:#1f2933;
  classDef juvenile fill:#fff3df,stroke:#c68519,stroke-width:2px,color:#1f2933;
  classDef predator fill:#fdf2e8,stroke:#c8523f,stroke-width:2px,color:#1f2933;
  classDef survival fill:#e8f6f2,stroke:#13856f,stroke-width:2px,color:#1f2933;
  class ICE,COLD,SST physical;
  class BLOOM,PREY prey;
  class A0,ENERGY,JLOC juvenile;
  class SEP,ADULT,OVER predator;
  class WINTER,PSURV,REC survival;
```

The generic graph is intentionally broader than the statistical examples. It
shows that a negative SST coefficient would be consistent with an energetic
constraint, but would not identify prey quality, age-0 energy, or overwinter
survival as the active mediator. Likewise, a cold-pool coefficient would be a
proxy for spatial separation and cannibalism unless overlap and mortality were
observed directly.

### Two illustrative hypotheses

The proof of concept compares two single-edge hypotheses with a common
reference:

- **Energetic-condition proxy:** higher age-0 late-summer SST is associated
  with lower age-1 recruitment because warmer conditions can increase
  metabolic demand and reduce fall energy reserves
  [@heintz2013; @siddon2013; @duffyanderson2016].
- **Spatial-separation proxy:** larger cold-pool extent is associated with
  higher age-1 recruitment because it can reduce juvenile-adult spatial
  overlap and cannibalism.

The age-0 SST value is carried forward to the DSEM row for that cohort's age-1
recruitment. The zero-lag path is therefore cohort-aligned rather than a claim
that SST was measured in the age-1 year. In this section "IID" refers to the
no-recruitment-edge reference model. The combined model is retained as a
limited diagnostic of whether the two proxy edges add information when fitted
together; it is not a third mechanistic hypothesis.

All four specifications use the same observation-year universe, missingness
pattern, standardization, and AR(1) processes for the observed covariates.
Within this common data block, AIC compares relative fit after accounting for
model complexity. The percentage reduction in residual recruitment variation
compares each model's estimated unexplained recruitment variance with the IID
reference. It is an in-sample description, not a causal R-squared or a
predictive-skill score.

### Illustrative results

```{r}
#| label: tbl-dsem-model-comparison
#| tbl-cap: "Illustrative Rceattle-DSEM model comparison. Delta AIC and the percentage reduction in residual recruitment variation are calculated within the common observation block."
#| tbl-pos: "H"

dsem_summary |>
  select(
    Model,
    AIC,
    `Delta AIC`,
    `Residual variation reduced (%)`
  ) |>
  arrange(AIC) |>
  gt() |>
  fmt_number(columns = c(AIC, `Delta AIC`), decimals = 2) |>
  fmt_number(columns = `Residual variation reduced (%)`, decimals = 1) |>
  cols_width(
    Model ~ px(190),
    `Residual variation reduced (%)` ~ px(130),
    everything() ~ px(95)
  )
```

All four fits fully met the convergence criteria, had positive-definite Hessians, and had
maximum absolute gradients no larger than
`r format(max(dsem_summary$maximum_gradient), scientific = TRUE, digits = 2)`.
The age-0 late-summer SST model had the lowest AIC
and reduced estimated residual recruitment variation by
`r sprintf("%.1f", 100 * dsem_variance$variance_reduction_from_iid[dsem_variance$model == "late_summer_sst"])`%
relative to IID. The cold-pool-only model reduced residual variation by
`r sprintf("%.1f", 100 * dsem_variance$variance_reduction_from_iid[dsem_variance$model == "cold_pool"])`%
and had higher AIC than IID. The combined model reduced residual variation by
`r sprintf("%.1f", 100 * dsem_variance$variance_reduction_from_iid[dsem_variance$model == "combined"])`%,
but its additional parameter left its AIC above the SST-only model
(@tbl-dsem-model-comparison; @fig-dsem-aic).

```{r}
#| label: fig-dsem-aic
#| fig-cap: "Akaike information criterion differences for the illustrative DSEM models. The age-0 late-summer SST model has the lowest AIC."
#| fig-alt: "Horizontal bars compare delta AIC for the no-edge IID reference, cold pool, age-0 late-summer SST, and the combined proxy model. The SST-only model has the lowest AIC, followed by the combined model, IID, and cold-pool-only model."
#| out-width: "76%"
#| fig-align: center

knitr::include_graphics(dsem_aic_figure_file)
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-dsem-recruitment-paths
#| tbl-cap: "Standardized proxy paths to age-1 recruitment. Intervals are the estimate plus or minus 1.96 standard errors."
#| tbl-pos: "H"

dsem_recruitment_paths |>
  select(Model, Covariate, estimate, standard_error, lower_95, upper_95) |>
  gt(groupname_col = "Model") |>
  fmt_number(
    columns = c(estimate, standard_error, lower_95, upper_95),
    decimals = 3
  ) |>
  cols_label(
    estimate = "Estimate",
    standard_error = "Standard error",
    lower_95 = "Lower 95%",
    upper_95 = "Upper 95%"
  )
```

The SST coefficient was negative and its interval excluded zero in both the
single-edge and combined models. The cold-pool coefficient was small and its
interval included zero in both models. In plain language, the current annual data contain a modest
in-sample association consistent with the warm-year energetic-constraint
hypothesis, while the direct cold-pool proxy edge received little support.
Neither result establishes the intervening mechanism
(@tbl-dsem-recruitment-paths; @fig-dsem-edges).

```{r}
#| label: fig-dsem-edges
#| fig-cap: "Standardized coefficients for the illustrative DSEM models. Points are estimates and horizontal lines are 95% intervals. Blue edges describe temporal persistence in observed covariates; orange edges are the two direct proxy paths to age-1 recruitment."
#| fig-alt: "Four panels show standardized DSEM coefficients. Both environmental series have positive temporal persistence. Age-0 late-summer SST has a negative recruitment coefficient with its interval below zero, while the cold-pool recruitment coefficient is close to zero and its interval overlaps zero."
#| out-width: "100%"

knitr::include_graphics(dsem_edges_figure_file)
```

The missingness-preserving randomization check replaced both environmental
series with independent standard-normal values using seed
`r sprintf("%d", as.integer(dsem_random_design$seed))`. None of the randomized
recruitment paths improved on the randomized IID model: their delta AIC values
ranged from
`r sprintf("%.2f", min(dsem_random_summary[["Delta AIC"]][dsem_random_summary$model != "iid"]))`
to
`r sprintf("%.2f", max(dsem_random_summary[["Delta AIC"]][dsem_random_summary$model != "iid"]))`,
and every randomized path interval included zero. This is a basic check against
an identical signal arising from arbitrary series with the same gaps; it does
not replace out-of-sample validation.

### Interpretation and next test

This proof of concept supports keeping the candidate set small. The SST result
is useful as an illustration of the Rceattle-DSEM connection, but SST is an
upstream proxy. The next scientifically stronger test is to insert a proximal
mediator from the mechanism table: fall age-0 total energy or energy density,
followed by a lipid-rich large-copepod/euphausiid index when enough cohort years
are available [@eisner2020copepods; @heintz2013; @siddon2013]. That sequence
would test whether the SST association weakens when the hypothesized energetic
path is represented directly.

A top-down overlap example should return only after its timing and uncertainty
are aligned with the age-0-to-age-1 survival interval. The available
adult-pollock overlap product is informative, but its survey occurs after the
start-of-year age-1 state and it is partly population-derived. Including it here
would blur a causal example with a contemporaneous association.

Before either proxy is considered for operational recruitment inference, the
paths should be tested with terminal-year or blocked prediction, retrospective
stability, alternative cohort timing, and observation-error sensitivity.
These DSEM results remain separate from the assessment configuration and
projection results.

## Summary and conclusions

When Rceattle parameters and fishery selectivity are set to the values used in
the ADMB model, Rceattle reproduces spawning
biomass and predicted catch to numerical precision. This establishes
agreement in the tested population-dynamics calculations and parameter
mapping. When Rceattle is fit to the data, the trajectories differ more,
and the residual least-identified direction remains in the shared ATS/AVO
annual selectivity deviations. The added ATS/AVO coefficient-increment penalty
reduced the condition number below the convergence-warning threshold.

The diagnostic results identify a focused development path for the September
2026 Plan Team evaluation. The Rceattle fit fully met the convergence criteria.
Composition OSA residuals remain underdispersed.
Nine terminal-year-consistent peels converge successfully and produce
positive retrospective bias in spawning biomass, total biomass, and
recruitment, together with negative bias in fishing mortality. The historical
2D AR1 sensitivity did not converge and retains its research status. The
50-jitter diagnostic recovered the best solution 48 times and found a poorer
mode twice; the age-3+ natural-mortality profile is shallow.

The scaled-back DSEM proof of concept compared two prespecified proxy edges
with the no-edge IID reference. The age-0 late-summer SST model had the lowest
AIC and reduced estimated residual recruitment variation by
`r sprintf("%.1f", 100 * dsem_variance$variance_reduction_from_iid[dsem_variance$model == "late_summer_sst"])`%
relative to IID. The cold-pool edge received little support. This result
illustrates the Rceattle-DSEM connection, but the annual data do not yet
represent the prey, age-0 energy, overwinter-survival, and cannibalism
mediators required to attribute the association to a causal mechanism.

Immediate work should retain the ADMB-to-Rceattle comparison as a repeatable
numerical check, evaluate selectivity and survey influence on the retrospective
pattern, and continue sensitivity checks for the shared ATS/AVO annual
selectivity deviations. Given acceptance in other applications and the proven
bridging aspects, we feel this approach should be adopted for operational
management advice for November/December 2026. Future refinements will explore
trade-offs in fitting data in alternative ways (e.g., using random effects
approaches for selectivity variability, selecting alternatives to the
robust-multinomial approach used in this example). The exploratory DSEM work
provides a reproducible approach for adding cohort-aligned covariates, while
remaining separate from the final assessment configuration and projection
results.

Rceattle is broadly used beyond this EBS pollock application. The framework
has been applied to single- and multispecies groundfish cases in the eastern
Bering Sea and Gulf of Alaska, including configurations for pollock, Pacific
cod, and arrowtooth flounder. Its shared data structure accommodates one or
more stocks, one- or two-sex population dynamics, and multiple fisheries and
surveys. The present bridge therefore represents an application of a broader
assessment framework rather than a model developed only for EBS pollock.

Rceattle is also under active development. Continued work on its TMB model,
data interfaces, diagnostics, simulation tools, and documentation is expanding
the set of configurations that can be represented and tested. This development
is an advantage for future assessment work, but it also reinforces the need to
record package versions, preserve model inputs and fitted outputs, and repeat
the ADMB bridge and convergence checks when consequential components change.

Only part of the available Rceattle feature set was explored here. This study
focused on a single-species age-structured configuration, ADMB parameter
mapping, selectivity, composition fitting, standard diagnostics, projections,
and an exploratory DSEM extension. It did not fully evaluate joint multispecies
estimation, bioenergetics-based predation mortality, estimable growth,
environmental linkages across other biological parameters, alternative harvest
control rules and climate scenarios, or closed-loop management strategy
evaluation. These capabilities provide a substantial agenda for future testing,
but each should be evaluated through controlled sensitivities and diagnostics
before contributing to operational EBS pollock advice.

### A-1 Reproducibility and analysis sequence {.unnumbered}

The working paper is rendered from saved model and diagnostic products so that
building the document does not repeat long model fits. The commands below are
run from the project directory, in the order shown when an earlier product is
required by a later analysis.

1. The [input-preparation script](<2024 EBS pollock setup data.R>) documents
   the transformations used to prepare the aligned Rceattle workbook; its
   precursor workbook is regenerated with
   `Rscript "2024 EBS pollock setup data.R"`. The frozen workbook used for the
   reported fit is `Data/EBS_24_pollock_m23_rceattle_full_1964-2024.xlsx`.
   The same script documents the modified ADMB reference rebuild, run as
   `cd ADMB/m23_rceattle_full && admb pm && ./pm -nox -iprint 150` after the
   ADMB executable directory has been added to `PATH`.
2. The [two-stage fitting script](<2024 EBS pollock.R>) fits the reported
   Rceattle configuration and the 2D age-by-year AR1 sensitivity with
   `Rscript "2024 EBS pollock.R"`. The
   [5.8.1 summary script](R/finalize_rceattle_5_8_1_analysis.R) then
   generates the fitted-model summaries and standard-multinomial sensitivity
   using `Rscript R/finalize_rceattle_5_8_1_analysis.R`.
3. The [ADMB bridge runner](R/run_canonical_pm_forward_bridge.R) sets the
   Rceattle parameters and realized selectivity to the ADMB values and saves
   the trajectory, likelihood, and gradient comparisons with
   `Rscript R/run_canonical_pm_forward_bridge.R`.
4. The [OSA runner](R/run_canonical_pm_diagnostics.R) generates the saved OSA
   residuals with `Rscript R/run_canonical_pm_diagnostics.R`. The
   [retrospective script](<2024 EBS pollock two-stage retrospectives.R>) runs
   the nine terminal-year-consistent peels with
   `Rscript "2024 EBS pollock two-stage retrospectives.R"`.
5. The [5.8.1 self-test runner](R/run_rceattle_5_8_1_self_test.R) generates 50
   phased simulations with `Rscript R/run_rceattle_5_8_1_self_test.R`. The
   [restart runner](R/run_rceattle_5_8_1_self_test_restart.R) repeats the same
   simulations from the estimated solution with
   `Rscript R/run_rceattle_5_8_1_self_test_restart.R`, and the
   [validation summarizer](R/summarize_rceattle_5_8_1_validation.R) is run with
   `Rscript R/summarize_rceattle_5_8_1_validation.R`.
6. The [projection runner](R/run_spmr_tier3_projection.R), which uses the
   [Rceattle-to-SPM input writer](R/write_spmr_projection_inputs.R), generates
   the seven-scenario and fixed-catch projection products with
   `Rscript R/run_spmr_tier3_projection.R`.
7. The [DSEM script](<2024 EBS pollock DSEM proof of concept.R>) runs the four
   observed-covariate models with
   `Rscript "2024 EBS pollock DSEM proof of concept.R"` and the
   missingness-preserving randomized controls with
   `Rscript "2024 EBS pollock DSEM proof of concept.R" --randomized`.
8. After these saved products are available, the HTML and PDF are generated
   together with `quarto render ebswp.qmd`.

### A-2 Rceattle-to-spmR projection bridge {.unnumbered}

The projection bridge is a deterministic file adapter rather than a second
assessment fit. The [input writer](R/write_spmr_projection_inputs.R) reads the
saved `nonparametric_pm` Rceattle object, extracts the population state,
biological schedules, fishery schedule, and historical series needed by the
Standard Projection Model (SPM), and writes them in the SPM `pm.prj` format.
It also writes the projection controls in `spm.dat`. The
[projection runner](R/run_spmr_tier3_projection.R) passes those files to
`spmR::runSPM(..., engine = "admb")`, which executes the validated SPM binary
and returns the simulation-level output used by the report.

The adapter preserves the terminal assessment state and makes each conversion
explicit. Numbers at age, natural mortality, and the
weight schedules are passed on their Rceattle scales. With abundance in
millions of fish and weight in kilograms, their product has units of thousand
metric tons. Maturity is divided by its maximum, matching the SPM input
convention used for this stock. The spawning-month encodings differ by one
because Rceattle records elapsed months and SPM uses a one-based calendar
month; both represent survival through 0.25 of the year
(@tbl-spmr-bridge-fields).

```{r}
#| label: tbl-spmr-bridge-fields
#| tbl-cap: "Mapping from the saved Rceattle fit to the SPM species input file."
#| tbl-pos: "H"

tibble::tribble(
  ~SPM_field, ~Rceattle_source, ~Transformation_and_years,
  "Average recent F", "quantities: F_spp", "Arithmetic mean for 2020--2024; used by Alternative 3",
  "Natural mortality at age", "quantities: M_at_age", "Terminal-year schedule (2024)",
  "Maturity at age", "data_list: maturity", "Divided by its maximum to match the SPM convention",
  "Spawning weight at age", "data_list: weight and ssb_wt_index", "Terminal-year spawning-weight schedule",
  "Fishery weight at age", "data_list: weight, fishery index", "Terminal-year fishery-weight schedule",
  "Fishery selectivity at age", "quantities: sel_at_age for Fishery", "Arithmetic mean at each age for 2020--2024",
  "Terminal numbers at age", "quantities: N_at_age", "Terminal assessment state (2024)",
  "Recruitment history", "quantities: R", "Annual age-1 recruitment for 1978--2024",
  "Spawning-biomass history", "quantities: ssb", "Annual spawning biomass for 1977--2023",
  "Spawning month", "data_list: spawn_month = 3", "Written as SPM Spawnmo = 4; both equal 0.25 year"
) |>
  gt() |>
  cols_label(
    SPM_field = "SPM field",
    Rceattle_source = "Rceattle source",
    Transformation_and_years = "Transformation and years"
  ) |>
  cols_width(
    SPM_field ~ px(145),
    Rceattle_source ~ px(185),
    Transformation_and_years ~ px(280)
  )
```

Annual Rceattle fishery selectivity is already normalized to a mean of one
across ages. The projection schedule is calculated as the arithmetic mean at
each age across 2020--2024; averaging these normalized annual curves retains a
mean of one. This five-year schedule replaces the former terminal-year-only
curve. The writer saves the five contributing curves in
`fishery_selectivity_recent_years.csv`, the applied average in
`age_schedules.csv`, and the rule and exact years in `lineage.csv`. Thus the
projection input can be reconstructed without reading values back from the
formatted `pm.prj` file.

The `spm.dat` file starts projections in 2025, runs 14 projection years and
1,000 simulations, and requests all seven Tier 3 alternatives. Catch is fixed
at 1,350 thousand t in 2025 and 2026 before the alternatives diverge. A
separate call uses Alternative 2 with catch fixed at 1,300 thousand t for
2025--2032. The writer copies the validated SPM executable and `tacpar.dat`
control file into each run directory. `manifest.csv` records the role and
presence of every required input, while `lineage.csv` records the terminal
year, software versions, selectivity rule, and averaging years.

The saved products passed all file and field consistency checks. These checks
do not replace review of the harvest assumptions or the biological
appropriateness of a five-year selectivity average
(@tbl-spmr-bridge-checks).

The means formerly displayed in the long main-text table remain available as
a [downloadable CSV](results/canonical_pm/spmR_projection/spm_projection_means.csv){download="spm_projection_means.csv"}.
This file retains every alternative and projection year in a compact,
machine-readable form. The underlying simulation-level output remains in the
saved analysis products but is omitted from the report because of its size.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-spmr-bridge-checks
#| tbl-cap: "Automated consistency checks for the Rceattle-to-spmR projection bridge."
#| tbl-pos: "H"

selectivity_average_check <- spmr_selectivity_history |>
  group_by(Age) |>
  summarize(Selectivity = mean(Selectivity), .groups = "drop") |>
  left_join(
    spmr_age_schedules |> select(Age, Applied = Selectivity),
    by = "Age"
  )

expected_selectivity_years <- seq.int(
  spmr_lineage$terminal_year - spmr_lineage$fishery_selectivity_year_count + 1L,
  spmr_lineage$terminal_year
)

tibble(
  Check = c(
    "Required projection files",
    "Recent selectivity years",
    "Applied five-year selectivity mean",
    "Projection alternatives",
    "Projection start year"
  ),
  Result = c(
    if_else(all(spmr_manifest$exists), "Pass", "Fail"),
    if_else(
      identical(
        as.integer(sort(unique(spmr_selectivity_history$Year))),
        expected_selectivity_years
      ),
      "Pass", "Fail"
    ),
    if_else(
      max(abs(selectivity_average_check$Selectivity - selectivity_average_check$Applied)) < 1e-10,
      "Pass", "Fail"
    ),
    if_else(
      identical(as.integer(sort(unique(spmr_detail$Alt))), 1:7),
      "Pass", "Fail"
    ),
    if_else(
      min(spmr_detail$Year) == spmr_lineage$terminal_year + 1L,
      "Pass", "Fail"
    )
  ),
  Evidence = c(
    paste(sum(spmr_manifest$exists), "of", nrow(spmr_manifest), "manifest targets present"),
    paste(sort(unique(spmr_selectivity_history$Year)), collapse = ", "),
    paste0(
      "maximum absolute difference = ",
      format(max(abs(selectivity_average_check$Selectivity - selectivity_average_check$Applied)), scientific = TRUE)
    ),
    paste(sort(unique(spmr_detail$Alt)), collapse = ", "),
    as.character(min(spmr_detail$Year))
  )
) |>
  gt() |>
  tab_style(
    style = cell_text(weight = "bold"),
    locations = cells_body(columns = Result)
  )
```

The generic DAG in Section 7 serves as the initial full conceptual graph. The
fitted SST and cold-pool graphs are deliberately simplified descendants of
that graph, not a search across every available series. For November, each
candidate graph should be traceable to a row in the mechanism table and should
use the same analysis data block as the IID no-recruitment-edge reference. The
final ESP should then report the causal statement, lag, expected sign, data
limitations, path estimate, uncertainty, change in unexplained recruitment
variation, and predictive check for every retained recruitment edge.

Fishery performance and socioeconomic indicators can be transferred from the
SAFE after the biological indicator set is stable. They should occupy the
standard socioeconomic synthesis and monitoring subsections rather than be
inserted as recruitment causes unless a separate, defensible causal hypothesis
requires them. This division keeps the integrated Rceattle-DSEM analysis
focused on the population response while allowing the ESP appendix to inform
both biological risk and TAC considerations.

### A-4 Model fitting details {.unnumbered}

The fishery selectivity likelihood has multiple modes, so the reported
Rceattle configuration used data-based fishery-selectivity starting values and two fitting
stages. The first stage disabled the annual selectivity deviations to establish
the selectivity and abundance scale. The second stage restored the deviations
and used the first-stage solution as its initial values. This sequence produced
a small maximum gradient and fully met the convergence criteria. With the direct ATS/AVO
coefficient-increment penalty, the Hessian condition number was approximately
489,000; its weakest direction remained in the shared ATS/AVO annual
selectivity deviations (`sel_coff_dev`) rather than fishery/CPUE.

The complete fitting sequence, including the empirical starting values and
the two estimation stages, is in the
[two-stage fitting script](<2024 EBS pollock.R>) and is run with
`Rscript "2024 EBS pollock.R"`. The nine-peel implementation is in the
[retrospective script](<2024 EBS pollock two-stage retrospectives.R>) and is
run with `Rscript "2024 EBS pollock two-stage retrospectives.R"`.

The retrospective peels repeat this sequence after recalculating the data-based
selectivity starting values for each terminal year. Because `sel_coff_dev`
contains annual random-walk increments at age, each peel fixes the terminal-year
fishery and mirrored catch-per-unit-effort increments at zero. This holds their
terminal selectivity-at-age curves at the preceding-year curves. The completed
development components distinguish the accepted comparison, diagnostic work,
and unresolved research sensitivities (@tbl-initial-developments).

```{r}
#| label: tbl-initial-developments
#| tbl-cap: "Disposition of the Rceattle development components."

initial_development_status |>
  gt() |>
  cols_width(
    Item ~ px(35),
    Initial_development ~ px(120),
    September_review_result ~ px(170),
    Plan_Team_interpretation ~ px(190)
  ) |>
  cols_label(
    Initial_development = "Development component",
    September_review_result = "Review result",
    Plan_Team_interpretation = "Interpretation"
  ) |>
  tab_style(
    style = cell_text(weight = "bold"),
    locations = cells_body(columns = Item)
  )
```

### A-5 Jitter and natural-mortality profile {.unnumbered}

The [extended-diagnostics runner](R/run_rceattle_5_8_1_extended_diagnostics.R)
generates both the 50 jitter fits and the age-3-and-older natural-mortality
profile with `Rscript R/run_rceattle_5_8_1_extended_diagnostics.R`.
The [profile-component summarizer](R/summarize_rceattle_5_8_1_m_profile.R)
extracts the saved `jnll_comp` matrices without refitting the model and is run
with `Rscript R/summarize_rceattle_5_8_1_m_profile.R`.

The 50 phased jitter runs test sensitivity to dispersed starting values.
Forty-eight returned to the best objective within numerical precision. Two
received `WARN` status and reached an inferior mode with an objective increase
of approximately
`r sprintf("%.1f", max(jitter_summary$Delta_objective, na.rm = TRUE))`.
This reproduces the pre-existing multimodality and shows why convergence of one
run is not sufficient evidence that the global mode was found. Forty-eight
runs returned to the best mode and two reached the inferior mode
(@tbl-jitter-summary).

```{r}
#| label: tbl-jitter-summary
#| tbl-cap: "Rceattle 5.8.1 phased-jitter results for the fitted configuration. Delta objective is measured from the best of 50 runs."

jitter_summary |>
  mutate(
    Convergence_status = if_else(
      Convergence_status == "OK",
      "Criteria fully met",
      Convergence_status
    )
  ) |>
  group_by(Convergence_status) |>
  summarise(
    Runs = n(),
    Minimum_delta_objective = min(Delta_objective),
    Maximum_delta_objective = max(Delta_objective),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  gt() |>
  fmt_number(
    columns = c(Minimum_delta_objective, Maximum_delta_objective),
    decimals = 3
  ) |>
  cols_label(
    Convergence_status = "Status",
    Minimum_delta_objective = "Minimum delta objective",
    Maximum_delta_objective = "Maximum delta objective"
  )
```

The age-3-and-older natural-mortality profile was evaluated from 0.15 to 0.50.
The grid minimum occurred at
`r sprintf("%.2f", mortality_profile[["Age-3+ natural mortality"]][which.min(mortality_profile$Objective)])`,
but the objective changed by only
`r sprintf("%.2f", max(mortality_profile$Delta_objective))`
across the entire grid. The profile is therefore shallow and does not support
precise estimation of natural mortality from these data alone.

The saved profile fits retain Rceattle's full negative-log-likelihood (NLL)
component matrix. The component entries sum to the reported objective at every
grid point to within numerical precision. Each component is centered on its
value at the grid minimum of
`r sprintf("%.2f", mortality_profile_min_m)`. Positive changes indicate that a
component favors the lower grid-minimum value over the plotted value; negative
changes indicate that the component favors the plotted value. The total panel
is the sum of the data and penalty panels. The M-prior contribution is zero in
this configuration (@fig-natural-mortality-profile).

```{r}
#| label: fig-natural-mortality-profile
#| fig-cap: "Negative-log-likelihood components across the age-3-and-older natural-mortality profile. Each curve shows delta NLL relative to that component's value at M = 0.20. Positive values favor M = 0.20 over the plotted value; negative values favor the plotted value. Components in the three lower panels sum to the total objective change in the upper-left panel."
#| fig-alt: "Four-panel plot with M on the horizontal axis and delta NLL on the vertical axis. The total objective is shallow with a minimum at M equals 0.20. Index likelihood and both selectivity penalties rise toward M equals 0.50. Composition likelihood and initial-abundance penalties decline and partly offset that increase. Catch and recruitment-deviation components change little."
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 7
#| fig-pos: "H"

mortality_profile_components |>
  filter(Component %in% c(
    "Total objective",
    "Index data", "Catch data", "Composition data",
    "Non-parametric selectivity", "Selectivity deviates",
    "Initial abundance deviates", "Recruitment deviates"
  )) |>
  mutate(
    Group = factor(
      Group,
      levels = c(
        "Total objective", "Data likelihoods",
        "Selectivity penalties", "Population penalties"
      )
    ),
    Component = recode(
      Component,
      `Non-parametric selectivity` = "Selectivity-curve penalty",
      `Selectivity deviates` = "Annual-selectivity penalty",
      `Initial abundance deviates` = "Initial-abundance penalty",
      `Recruitment deviates` = "Recruitment-deviation penalty"
    )
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(
    x = `Age-3+ natural mortality`,
    y = Delta_component,
    color = Component,
    shape = Component
  )) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "gray55", linetype = 2) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  facet_wrap(vars(Group), ncol = 2, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_color_brewer(type = "qual", palette = "Dark2") +
  labs(
    x = expression(M),
    y = expression(Delta*"NLL"),
    color = NULL,
    shape = NULL
  ) +
  ggthemes::theme_few() +
  theme(
    legend.position = "bottom",
    legend.key.width = grid::unit(1.2, "lines")
  ) +
  guides(
    color = guide_legend(nrow = 3, byrow = TRUE),
    shape = guide_legend(nrow = 3, byrow = TRUE)
  )
```

The increase in total NLL from \(M=0.20\) to \(M=0.50\) was
`r sprintf("%.2f", mortality_profile$Objective[mortality_profile[["Age-3+ natural mortality"]] == mortality_profile_compare_m] - min(mortality_profile$Objective))`.
The strongest single counterweight
was the BTS age-composition likelihood, which improved by
`r sprintf("%.2f", abs(mortality_profile_contribution[["BTS age-composition likelihood"]]))`
NLL units as M increased. Lower M was favored mainly by the ATS age-composition
likelihood, the BTS index likelihood, and the selectivity penalties. Because
ATS and AVO share a selectivity index in this configuration, the shared
ATS/AVO penalties are stored in the AVO-labeled column of `jnll_comp`
(@tbl-natural-mortality-profile-components).

```{r}
#| label: tbl-natural-mortality-profile-components
#| tbl-cap: "Material fleet-specific contributions to the total NLL change from M = 0.20 to M = 0.50. The direction column identifies the M value favored by each term; positive contributions favor lower M and negative contributions favor higher M. Terms with absolute contributions below 0.25 NLL units are omitted."
#| tbl-pos: "H"

mortality_profile_material_contributions |>
  gt() |>
  fmt_number(columns = `NLL contribution`, decimals = 2) |>
  cols_label(Direction = "Direction favored") |>
  cols_width(
    Term ~ px(320),
    Direction ~ px(115),
    `NLL contribution` ~ px(110)
  ) |>
  tab_style(
    style = cell_text(weight = "bold"),
    locations = cells_body(columns = Direction)
  )
```

This decomposition shows that the low profile minimum is a trade-off among
specific survey, composition, and selectivity terms rather than a uniform
signal for lower natural mortality. It also explains why this result can
differ from natural-mortality analyses that use different composition
likelihoods, survey weights, or selectivity penalties. A direct comparison
with those analyses should match these components and their weights before
interpreting the difference as biological evidence about M.

```{=latex}
\clearpage
```

### A-6 2D age-by-year AR1 selectivity sensitivity {.unnumbered}

The penalized-effects initialization and subsequent Laplace fit are in the
[two-stage fitting script](<2024 EBS pollock.R>) and are run with
`Rscript "2024 EBS pollock.R"`. A separate
[fixed-scale follow-up](<2024 EBS pollock 2D AR1 fixed sd test.R>) can be run
with `Rscript "2024 EBS pollock 2D AR1 fixed sd test.R"`; it is a development
check and is not the sensitivity summarized below.

The 2D AR1 sensitivity applied an age-by-year field to the shared fishery and
catch-per-unit-effort selectivity block over 1964--2024. The age-year deviations
were first fit as penalized effects to initialize the field and then integrated
as random effects with a Laplace approximation. The initialized Laplace fit
failed the gradient, Hessian, and bound checks. The estimated correlation and
scale parameters are retained only as diagnostics
(@tbl-ar1-selectivity-parameter-summary).

```{r}
#| label: tbl-ar1-selectivity-parameter-summary
#| tbl-cap: "Diagnostic 2D AR1 fishery-selectivity correlation and scale estimates."
#| tbl-pos: "H"

ar1_selectivity_parameter_summary |>
  select(-Final_internal_value) |>
  gt() |>
  fmt_number(
    columns = c(
      Penalized_effects_initialization,
      Final_random_effects_fit
    ),
    decimals = 3
  ) |>
  cols_label(
    Quantity = "Quantity",
    Internal_parameter = "Rceattle parameter",
    Penalized_effects_initialization = "Penalized effects",
    Final_random_effects_fit = "Random-effects fit"
  ) |>
  tab_source_note(
    source_note = paste(
      "Correlations are on the -1 to 1 scale; the deviation scale is a",
      "positive standard deviation. The fit failed convergence checks."
    )
  )
```

The failed random-effects fit had a maximum marginal gradient of 19.7 on
`rec_pars`, a non-invertible Hessian, 61 `log_F` parameters at their configured
bounds, and `FAIL` convergence status. Its selectivity surfaces differ visibly
from both the ADMB reference and accepted Rceattle configuration, but the
failed fit precludes biological interpretation
(@fig-development-selectivity-ridges).

```{r}
#| label: fig-development-selectivity-ridges
#| fig-cap: "Development comparison of relative fishery selectivity for ADMB, the Rceattle configuration, and the failed 2D age-by-year AR1 sensitivity."
#| fig-alt: "Three side-by-side ridge plots compare relative fishery selectivity by age and year for ADMB, the Rceattle configuration, and the failed 2D age-by-year AR1 sensitivity."
#| fig-width: 15
#| fig-height: 10
#| out-width: "100%"

ggplot(
  selectivity_ridges,
  aes(
    x = Age,
    y = Year_factor,
    height = Relative_selectivity,
    fill = Model
  )
) +
  ggridges::geom_ridgeline(
    scale = 3.8,
    alpha = 0.28,
    color = "black",
    linewidth = 0.2,
    show.legend = FALSE
  ) +
  facet_wrap(vars(Model), nrow = 1) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(
    "ADMB reference" = "#1f78b4",
    "Rceattle NonParametricPM" = "#1b9e77",
    "Rceattle 2D AR1 (failed)" = "#d95f02"
  )) +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(1, 15), breaks = 1:15) +
  labs(x = "Age", y = "Year") +
  ggthemes::theme_few() +
  theme(
    strip.text = element_text(face = "bold"),
    panel.spacing.x = grid::unit(1.2, "lines")
  )
```

### A-7 Acronyms {.unnumbered}

This appendix follows the glossary convention in the [Alaska Stock Assessment
Report (`asar`) package](https://github.com/nmfs-ost/asar)
[@schiano2026asar]. The project glossary uses ASAR's `\newacronym` format and
adds terms specific to this Rceattle comparison. The quoted label "PM" is a
model name. The glossary defines the abbreviations used throughout the report
(@tbl-acronyms).

```{r}
#| label: tbl-acronyms
#| tbl-cap: "Acronyms used in this working paper."

project_glossary |>
  select(Acronym, Definition) |>
  gt::gt() |>
  gt::cols_width(
    Acronym ~ gt::px(105),
    Definition ~ gt::pct(75)
  )
```
